title: The lamb (Exodus 12)
hook: blood on the doorposts, unleavened bread, eaten in haste; Christians call Jesus our Passover

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rerum Novarum: bricks without straw, nine plagues, and a heart that kept hardening. Your line was this is the finger of God.

A meal eaten standing up. Belt fastened, sandals on, walking stick in hand, as if you might have to leave mid-bite. Roast lamb, flat bread with no yeast because there's no time for dough to rise, bitter herbs. And outside, on the frame of the door, a smear of blood. That's the night before Israel leaves Egypt. And its name is still in a Catholic church every Easter: on the tall candle, in the songs, in the word for the whole mystery of Christ's death and rising.
screen: `A MEAL EATEN STANDING UP.` → `BLOOD ON THE DOOR FRAME.` → `A NAME STILL HEARD AT EASTER.`

segments.voice: First, each household takes a lamb, a year old, without blemish. On the fourteenth day of the month, at evening, they kill it, and with a bunch of hyssop brush its blood on the two doorposts and the lintel. They eat it roasted, with unleavened bread, in haste. Second, the night. This is the tenth plague, and the hardest page in Exodus: the death of the firstborn of Egypt. The text doesn't look away from the grief; there was a great cry in Egypt, it says, with no house where there was not one dead. But where God sees the blood on the door, God passes over. In Hebrew the feast is Pesach. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, calls it the Phase, that is, the Passage of the Lord. Third, the remembering. This day shall be a memorial, God says; keep it as a feast forever. Jews still keep Passover every spring at the Seder table, telling this night to their children. Fourth, the word Catholics took from it: Pasch. In Latin and Greek one word, pascha, names both Passover and Easter. Jesus ate his last supper at Passover time, and John's Gospel places his death on the day of Preparation for the Passover, when the lambs were being made ready. Paul writes to the Corinthians: "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." At the Vigil, the Easter Proclamation sings that this is the night the true Lamb is slain, whose blood marks the doorposts of believers. The paschal candle, the paschal mystery: every time a Catholic hears that word, it carries a lamb, a door, and a family eating in their traveling clothes.
screen: `A LAMB WITHOUT BLEMISH.` · `WHERE GOD SEES THE BLOOD, GOD PASSES OVER.` · `A MEMORIAL, KEPT FOREVER.` · `CHRIST OUR PASCH.`

segments.voice: Look at what's on your plate, now or at your next meal, before you begin: who grew it, carried it, cooked it, then take one bite and actually taste it. If you pray, give thanks before you eat, in your own way or with the Church's grace before meals; if you don't, simply give the food your full attention.
Pasch. From Hebrew Pesach, the Passover: the lamb, the blood on the door, the night of leaving. For Catholics, also Easter. Today's word.
Your line: the lord's passover. One word for Passover and Easter. Day three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, Catholics light the paschal candle and hear the Exsultet, which calls Easter night the night of the true Lamb, and Exodus 12 is read every Holy Thursday at the Mass of the Lord's Supper.

original.note: Hebrew: Passover, from a verb meaning to pass over or spare. Greek and Latin made it pascha, the Church's word for Easter.

chat.says: Why do Catholics call Easter things paschal, like the paschal candle?
options: Pascha names both Passover and Easter: Christ our pasch, the true Lamb.
It's Latin for candle, so the paschal candle just means the big candle.
It's the name of the saint who first lit a candle at the Easter Vigil.
